1:
Ellicott sets the chapter against the one before it, that having ended by allowing disqualified priests to eat of the sacrifices it now lays down when even qualified priests must not. Gill puts the same point the other way, that a blemish did not bar a man from the holy things but legal impurity barred everyone, and Henry adds the rabbinic detail that blemished priests were kept from idleness in the wood-room, picking out worm-eaten timber unfit for the altar. Calvin asks why a rule already binding on all Israel had to be enacted again for the priests, and answers that men placed in honour are apt to make God's favour a pretext, so that an express law was needed lest sacerdotal dignity become a cover for scandal. Clarke widens it further, that the chapter requires perfection in the offering as well as in the offerer, since the law admitted neither an imperfect gift nor an imperfect giver.

Henry divides the defilements into the lasting and the passing, leprosy or an issue on the one hand and the touch of a corpse on the other, and observes that what merely separated a layman from the sanctuary made a priest not more excusable but more abominable. Keil and Delitzsch run through the list as the text gives it, the leper, the man with an issue, the man defiled by a corpse, and whoever had touched an unclean creature or an unclean person. Ellicott corrects two renderings along the way, that the man of whom uncleanness may be taken is simply a man who is unclean and imparts it by contact, and that the soul which touches is here the priest, as the old Chaldee version says outright. Gill supplies the rabbinic measure from Jarchi, that a creeping thing defiled by so little as the bulk of a lentil.

The penalty is stated in a form Ellicott notices as unique, since Leviticus elsewhere always threatens that a soul shall be cut off from his people and here alone from God's presence. He takes the exceptional wording as fitted to the case, that a priest who approaches presumptuously will be banished by God himself as Nadab and Abihu were, and Henry reaches the same figure independently, that nearness to God is no security but an exposure, since the destruction comes from his presence. Wesley reads the cutting off as excommunication, excluding the man both from administering the ordinances and from partaking of them. Ellicott adds how the second Temple understood the death threatened, not as a sentence for any earthly court but as inflicted by the hand of heaven, which the Targum of Jonathan renders as a flaming fire.

What made the rule hard was that the holy things were the priest's living, and three sources say so. Ellicott points out that a defiled priest had to go without food until sundown, Wesley that this necessity is why his penalty was no longer than a layman's although his person was more sacred, and Henry that a man with most to lose by defilement has most reason to guard against it. Keil and Delitzsch narrow which gifts are meant, not the furniture of the sanctuary but the heave-offerings and wave-offerings assigned to the priests for maintenance, which they were not to treat as though they were common. Henry draws the design out of the whole, that the law taught the people reverence when they saw the priests themselves held off, and warns against the particular danger the text names, of profaning God's name in the very things we hallow to him.
10:
Gill, Ellicott and Wesley agree that the stranger here is not a foreigner but any man outside the priestly family, an Israelite or even a Levite. Clarke and Ellicott identify the sojourner and the hired servant from later Jewish usage as the Hebrew whose ear was pierced and the Hebrew hired by the year, neither the priest's property though his labour was. Calvin gives the rule a motive the others do not, that it aimed less at keeping strangers out than at forestalling priestly avarice, which would have driven a trade in the offerings and made the priest's house a provision-market. Without such a distinction, he argues, the people would soon have concluded that sacred food differed in nothing from common.

The bought slave was another matter, and Keil and Delitzsch explain why, that he became a member of the household and had been formally incorporated into the nation by circumcision. Ellicott adds that such a slave shared every Israelite privilege including the passover, and that the second Temple extended the right to a servant brought as dowry and to slaves the priest's slaves had bought. Gill reports that some rabbis inferred the priest's wife might eat because she too was bought with his money, and prefers the better reason that marriage made her a principal of the family. Clarke turns the verse against his own century, granting that Moses permitted slavery under restrictions but insisting a slave reckoned part of the priest's family was far better placed than those held by European Christians who quote this law to justify themselves.

Henry finds the sons no difficulty and the daughters a distinction, since a priest's daughter ate at her father's table until she married outside the family. Keil and Delitzsch explain the exception by household rather than descent, a childless widow returning home being of her father's family again, while one with children had formed a family of her own. Ellicott allows her the heave-offerings but not the wave-breast and heave-shoulder, and reports two later rulings, that she may not eat while reserved for a husband's brother or while carrying a child. Wesley explains the converse case, that the priest's wife eats though born elsewhere because a wife passes into her husband's privileges, and Clarke notes from Ward that widows in Bengal still return to their fathers.

For the man who ate unwittingly, Ellicott stresses the proportion of the penalty, a fifth added to the value being caution enough where withholding the holy things altogether required a trespass offering besides. He and Wesley agree the restitution is of the equivalent, the thing itself having been eaten. Calvin asks why the priests should be compensated at all, when men who let sacred things fall into contempt deserved punishment rather than payment. His answer is that the fault addressed is the layman's failure to reserve the priest's lawful portion, and that the point throughout is to keep what was offered to God from passing into common use.

Who bears the guilt is the last question, and Calvin takes the closing words as addressed to the priests, a mediator's impiety being a common iniquity that brings guilt on everyone. Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch read them the same way, that the priests must guard the offerings so carefully that no layman contracts sin through their negligence. Henry offers that sense and a second, that since the priests' eating of the sin-offering signified their bearing the congregation's iniquity, no stranger may presume to bear it, and those who set up mediators besides Christ rob him of his honour. He closes with two qualifications, that necessity could dispense with the law as when David ate the shewbread, and that ministers are still to take out the precious from the vile.
17:
Keil and Delitzsch state the rule plainly, that a sacrifice offered by Israelite or foreigner, for a vow or as a freewill gift, had to be faultless and male to win God's good pleasure for the offerer. Henry catalogues what counted as a blemish, blindness, lameness, a wen or the mange, and what the Jewish writers took the bruised and crushed to mean, namely castration. Ellicott observes that the list answers item by item to the defects which disqualify a priest in the preceding chapter, the maimed and the wen being explained by the second Temple as an injured eyebrow and a diseased eye. Gill shows the rule was not peculiar to Israel, citing the Egyptians who examined their bulls, the Romans who chose sheep in which nothing was wanting, and Homer's perfect goats.

The phrase rendered at your own will divides the sources. Calvin denies the rendering outright, holding the word can only point to God's good pleasure, so that they must beware of defect if they wish their offerings approved. He then allows the other reading if taken of God's gratuitous favour, since our services please him only as far as his indulgence awards them a worth they do not have, and ends with Christ washing out the blemishes of sacrifices that are the fruits of true regeneration. Ellicott and Gill reach the same result by translation rather than theology, and Wesley notes the male was required for the burnt offering only, females being accepted for peace and sin offerings.

The concession to freewill offerings produces the chapter's real difficulty. Henry takes the text as it stands, that a merely disproportioned animal might serve for a freewill gift though not for a vow, and draws from it that what was in our power before a vow is not afterwards. Calvin agrees a greater licence belongs where a man is under no obligation, while denying that any notably defective victim is acceptable, and Clarke reports the Jewish view that such animals never reached the altar but were sold for the sanctuary. Ellicott presses hardest, that the lawgiver can hardly contradict himself within three verses, that the second Temple read the verse as consecration for repairs, and that the text is probably disarranged and originally forbade the freewill offering too.

On the castrated animal Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree the four terms name the four ancient methods of the operation. Both insist the closing clause forbids the practice itself and not merely the offering, Keil and Delitzsch arguing against Clericus and Knobel that the words in your land cannot mean the preparing of sacrifices, since these were never prepared abroad. Ellicott adds that the prohibition still binds orthodox Jews, and that their teachers had lately debated it because it bears hard on those who farm. Keil and Delitzsch ground the whole rule in the plainest reason, that to castrate is to mutilate God's creation.

Whether the last verse concerns Gentile offerings or Israelite purchases is disputed, and Calvin and Ellicott both decide against the Jewish canonists. Calvin objects that the rabbinic reading founders on the closing words, which say the sacrifice would not be accepted from the Jews themselves, and takes the verse as a precaution lest a man think a defective beast permissible because he bought rather than bred it. He notes too that the offerings are called the bread of God, not because God eats, but so that men handling his table take more care than with an earthly prince's. Henry turns from rule to type, that a law requiring an unblemished victim fitted these sacrifices to prefigure the Lamb without blemish, and that Pilate in finding no fault pronounced the sacrifice sound without knowing it.
26:
Keil and Delitzsch explain the seven days under the dam by the maturity of the creature, which has not reached a self-sustained life within its first week, and note that Roman practice fixed similar intervals for pigs, sheep and oxen. They add that the week is the period sanctified by creation, a reason Calvin considers and dismisses as too subtle, since on that ground the seventh day rather than the eighth would be fittest, and holds instead that the point is simply maturity, as with circumcision. Calvin also finds two purposes in the rule, that an offering taken straight from the womb would be a fraudulent one, and that men who ate such sacrifices would grow accustomed to cruelty. Ellicott reports two rulings the second Temple built on the wording, that an animal delivered by artificial aid was disqualified, and that one whose mother died within the week could never be offered at all.

Clarke spends his note on the translation instead, protesting that an ox is a bull castrated so that a bullock was never yet brought forth, and that the word here plainly means a calf. He says outright that only his rule of printing the common version exactly restrains him from correcting the text, and adds on his own account that the flesh of very young animals is poor food and that there is something brutish in eating a creature before its hoofs are formed. On the dam and her young the sources agree the motive is mercy, Keil and Delitzsch grounding it in the relation God established between parent and offspring, Clarke in the duty of not blunting our moral feelings when we must take an animal's life, and Wesley simply in the savour of cruelty. Ellicott quotes the Chaldee, which prefaces the command with an address to Israel to be merciful on earth as their Father is merciful in heaven.

Calvin argues the verse is primarily about sacrifice rather than diet, since the chapter treats of offerings throughout and closes on the hallowing of God's name, though he will not contest a wider reading that would make it a supplement to the sixth commandment. His own conclusion is that God will not have the exercises of religion separated from the duties of humanity, and that his altar should not be a Cyclopean slaughter-house. Gill notes the rabbinic limitation of the rule to the female, so that Jarchi allows the killing of a sire and his young on one day. For the thank-offering, Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott agree that eating it the same day marks it as the first class of peace offering, and Ellicott repeats his preferred rendering, that it is offered for the offerer's acceptance rather than at his own will.

Ellicott objects to the conjunctions of the closing charge, holding that rendering them as therefore and neither is unnecessary and mars the simple and dignified style of the original. Clarke defines the profaning of God's name as treating his commands the way we treat other men's when no self-interest recommends them, and takes a second grievance with the translators over the phrase children of Israel, which he would render posterity, since children misleads the young into thinking little ones are meant. Calvin makes the profanation broader still, that every fancy men devise is a profanation and that the religion of the superstitious is full of sacrilege however well it pleases them. He and Wesley both read the mutual clause carefully, Calvin that God requires to be hallowed even as he hallows the people, and Wesley that God is hallowed either by Israel in keeping his commands or upon them in executing his judgments.
